blocks.md: **Duplicates die by SORTING + level-local first-use rule: among equal siblings, take only the first.**

blocks.label: Combination Sum II core (LC40)
blocks.py:
def comb(i, rem, c, cur, out):
    if rem == 0: out.append(cur[:]); return
    for j in range(i, len(c)):
        if c[j] > rem: break
        if j > i and c[j] == c[j-1]: continue   # killer line
        cur.append(c[j]); comb(j+1, rem-c[j], c, cur, out); cur.pop()
# sorted candidates prerequisite

items.title: Combination Sum II
items.statement: Each candidate once; unique combos; narrate the skip-line proof.

solutionCode.label: sort, then skip equal candidates at the SAME level

items.complexity: Time O(2^n * k) to enumerate and copy. Space O(n) depth. Sorting first is O(n log n) and is a prerequisite, not an optimisation.

followups.a: At one level of the tree, the loop chooses which candidate occupies this slot. Two equal candidates in that slot produce identical subtrees, so the second is redundant. `i > start` restricts the skip to siblings — the first candidate at each level is always allowed, which is what lets a duplicate still be *used* deeper via the i+1 recursion. Skipping without that guard would forbid [1,1] entirely.

followups.q: Why sort rather than dedupe the output?
followups.a: Deduping means generating exponentially many duplicates and then hashing them all — the work is done and thrown away. Sorting groups equals adjacently so the skip line prunes those subtrees before they are ever built. It is pruning versus filtering, and at n = 20 the difference is decisive.

items.title: Subsets II
items.statement: Power set with dups, output unique subsets.
hints: Same loop-skip inside pick-not-pick converted to for-form.

solutionCode.label: the same skip line, in for-loop form

followups.q: Why is the emit at the top of the function rather than at a leaf?
followups.a: In the for-loop form there is no "not pick" branch — declining to extend simply means the loop ends. So every node of the tree already represents a complete valid subset, and the emit belongs on entry. The pick/not-pick form emits only at depth n; the loop form emits at every node. Same set, different traversal.

followups.q: What does the skip line prevent concretely?
followups.a: On [1,2,2], without it you generate [1,2] twice — once picking the first 2, once the second. The skip line lets only the first 2 start a branch at that level, while [2,2] is still reachable because the deeper call starts at i+1 where the guard does not apply.

items.title: Permutations II

solutionCode.label: used[] plus the "previous equal must be placed first" rule
solutionCode.py:
def permute_unique(a: list) -> list:
    arr = sorted(a)                # MANDATORY: equals must be adjacent
    n = len(arr)
    used = [False] * n
    out, cur = [], []

    def rec():
        if len(cur) == n:
            out.append(cur[:])
            return
        for i in range(n):
            if used[i]:
                continue
            # Among equal values, enforce a fixed order: i may only be placed if
            # the identical value at i-1 is ALREADY placed.
            if i > 0 and arr[i] == arr[i - 1] and not used[i - 1]:
                continue
            used[i] = True
            cur.append(arr[i])
            rec()
            cur.pop()
            used[i] = False

    rec()
    return out

items.complexity: Time O(n * n!) worst case, far less with duplicates. Space O(n) for the used array plus O(n) depth.

followups.a: It forces equal values to be consumed left to right. If the earlier copy is not yet placed, this copy must wait — so a group of k equal values is only ever placed in one order, collapsing k! identical permutations into one. Flipping the condition to `used[i-1]` also deduplicates, but by the mirrored rule; either works as long as it is consistent.

followups.q: Why does this need `used[]` when R301 and R302 used a start index?
followups.a: Permutations may pick elements in any order, so there is no monotone "start" to advance — an element skipped now can still be used later. The used array tracks membership instead of position, which is what distinguishes permutation backtracking from combination backtracking.

items.title: Beautiful Arrangement
hints: Place position-by-position with immediate validity check.

solutionCode.label: check validity AT placement, not at the leaf

items.complexity: Time far below O(n!) because invalid branches die at placement; roughly O(k) where k is the number of valid arrangements. Space O(n).

followups.q: Why check validity at placement rather than at the leaf?
followups.a: A leaf check explores all n! arrangements and rejects most at the end. Checking at placement kills an entire subtree the instant a position is filled badly — for n = 15 that is the difference between 1.3 trillion arrangements and about 24,679 valid ones found in milliseconds. Prune as early as the constraint permits.

followups.q: Would filling positions in a different order help?
followups.a: Yes. Positions with fewest legal values are the most constraining, so filling those first prunes hardest — the "most constrained variable" heuristic from constraint solving. Ascending order is simple and adequate here; on larger n, ordering by candidate count is a real speedup.

items.title: Palindrome Partitioning
hints: isPal helper fine at this size.

solutionCode.label: cut tree: every prefix that is a palindrome opens a branch

items.complexity: Time O(n * 2^n) — up to 2^(n-1) cut positions, each costing O(n) to validate and copy. Space O(n) depth.

followups.q: What exactly is the tree branching on?
followups.a: Where to place the next cut. At position start, each choice of end gives a prefix s[start..end]; if that prefix is a palindrome the branch is legal and recursion continues after it. So the tree is over cut positions, not over characters — n-1 possible cuts gives the 2^(n-1) upper bound.

followups.q: How would you speed up the palindrome test?
followups.a: Precompute a DP table isPal[i][j] in O(n^2), turning each check from O(n) into O(1) and the total from O(n * 2^n) to O(2^n). At n = 16 the checks stop being the bottleneck. Worth mentioning even when the constraint does not demand it.

items.title: Rat in a Maze — print all paths
items.statement: DLRU ordered path strings through open cells.
hints: Lexicographic order via direction array order D,L,R,U.

solutionCode.label: mark, recurse in D-L-R-U order, unmark
solutionCode.py:
def find_paths(grid: list) -> list:
    n = len(grid)
    if n == 0 or grid[0][0] == 0:
        return []
    g = [row[:] for row in grid]
    out, path = [], []
    # D, L, R, U -- this order makes the output lexicographically sorted
    moves = [(1, 0, "D"), (0, -1, "L"), (0, 1, "R"), (-1, 0, "U")]

    def rec(r, c):
        if r == n - 1 and c == n - 1:
            out.append("".join(path))
            return
        g[r][c] = 0                      # MARK visited (block the cell)
        for dr, dc, ch in moves:
            nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
            if 0 <= nr < n and 0 <= nc < n and g[nr][nc]:
                path.append(ch)
                rec(nr, nc)
                path.pop()
        g[r][c] = 1                      # UNMARK -- other paths may reuse it

    rec(0, 0)
    return out

items.complexity: Time O(4^(n*m)) worst case; heavily pruned by walls and the visited marks. Space O(n*m) for the visited grid plus O(n*m) depth.

followups.q: Why must the cell be unmarked on the way out?
followups.a: The mark means "this cell is on the CURRENT path", not "this cell has ever been visited". A different path may legitimately pass through it. Leaving it blocked turns the search into a single-visit flood fill and silently loses most paths — the classic backtracking-versus-visited-set confusion.

followups.q: Why does D-L-R-U give sorted output?
followups.a: The direction letters happen to be in alphabetical order, and the recursion explores them in that order. Since paths are compared character by character, exploring branches in alphabetical order emits them in lexicographic order — no sort needed afterwards. Change the array order and you must sort.

items.title: Word Search in Grid

solutionCode.label: temporarily overwrite the cell as its own visited mark

items.complexity: Time O(rows * cols * 4^L) for a word of length L. Space O(L) depth — no extra visited grid needed.

followups.q: Why overwrite the cell instead of keeping a visited grid?
followups.a: It saves O(rows*cols) memory and one indirection per check. The sentinel just has to be a character that cannot appear in the word — '#' works because the board holds letters. Saving and restoring the original is what makes it a backtracking mark rather than destruction.

followups.q: Why check the index base case before the bounds check?
followups.a: When the last character matches, the next call is made with idx == len(word) but possibly out-of-bounds coordinates. Testing idx first returns true immediately; testing bounds first would reject a completed match that happened to walk off the edge. Order of guards is load-bearing here.
